{{Short description|Boundary layer that forms on a wedge}}
[[File:WedgeFlow.png|thumb|Wedge flow.]]
In fluid dynamics, the '''Falkner–Skan boundary layer''' (named after Victor Montague Falkner and [[Sylvia Skan|Sylvia W. Skan]]<ref>Falkner, V. M. and Skan, S. W., (1930).  ''[[Aeronautical Research Council Reports and Memoranda|Aero. Res. Coun. Rep. and Mem.]]'' no 1314.</ref>) describes the steady two-dimensional laminar [[boundary layer]] that forms on a wedge, i.e. flows in which the plate is not parallel to the flow. It is also representative of flow on a flat plate with an imposed pressure gradient along the plate length, a situation often encountered in wind tunnel flow.  It is a generalization of the flat plate [[Blasius boundary layer]] in which the pressure gradient along the plate is zero.



==Prandtl's boundary layer equations==

The basis of the Falkner-Skan approach are the [[Boundary layer#Boundary layer equations|Prandtl boundary layer equations]].  [[Ludwig Prandtl]]<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Prandtl|first1=L.|title=Über Flüssigkeitsbewegung bei sehr kleiner Reibung|journal=Verhandlinger 3. Int. Math. Kongr. Heidelberg|date=1904|pages=484–491}}</ref>  simplified the equations for fluid flowing along a wall (wedge) by dividing the flow into two areas: one close to the wall dominated by [[viscosity]], and one outside this near-wall boundary layer region where viscosity can be neglected without significant effects on the solution. This means that about half of the terms in the [[Navier-Stokes equations]] are negligible in near-wall boundary layer flows (except in a small region near the leading edge of the plate). This reduced set of equations are known as the [[Boundary layer#Boundary layer equations|Prandtl boundary layer equations]]. For steady [[incompressible flow]] with constant viscosity and density, these read:

Mass Continuity: <math> \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y}=0 </math>

<math>x</math>-Momentum: <math> u \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + v \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = - \dfrac{1}{\rho} \dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x} + {\nu} \dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} </math>

<math>y</math>-Momentum: <math> 0 = -  \dfrac{\partial p}{\partial y} </math>

Here the coordinate system is chosen with <math>x</math> pointing parallel to the plate in the direction of the flow and the <math>y</math> coordinate pointing towards the free stream, <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> are the <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> velocity components, <math>p</math> is the [[pressure]], <math>\rho</math> is the [[density]] and <math>\nu</math> is the [[viscosity|kinematic viscosity]].
  
A number of similarity solutions to these equations have been found for various types of flow. Falkner and Skan developed the similarity solution for the case of laminar flow along a wedge in 1930. The term ''similarity'' refers to the property that the velocity profiles at different positions in the flow look similar apart from scaling factors in the boundary layer thickness and a characteristic boundary layer velocity. These scaling factors reduce the [[partial differential equations]] to a set of relatively easily solved set of [[ordinary differential equations]].  

==Falkner–Skan equation - First order boundary layer==

Source:<ref>Rosenhead, Louis, ed. Laminar boundary layers. Clarendon Press, 1963.</ref>

Falkner and Skan generalized the [[Blasius boundary layer]] by considering a wedge with an angle of  <math> \pi \beta / 2 </math> from some uniform velocity field <math> U_0 </math>.  Falkner and Skan's first key assumption was that the pressure gradient term in the Prandtl ''x''-momentum equation could be replaced by the differential form of the [[Bernoulli effect|Bernoulli equation]] in the high [[Reynolds number]] limit.<ref>Falkner, V. M. and Skan, S. W., (1930).</ref>  Thus: 
:<math> -\dfrac{1}{\rho}\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x} = u_e \dfrac{d u_e}{dx} \quad .</math>
Here <math>u_e(x)</math> is the velocity of at the boundary layer edge and is the solution the [[Euler equations (fluid dynamics)]] in the outer region.

Having made the [[Bernoulli effect|Bernoulli equation]] substitution, Falkner and Skan pointed out that similarity solutions are obtained when the boundary layer thickness and velocity scaling factors are assumed to be simple power functions of ''x''.<ref>Falkner, V. M. and Skan, S. W., (1930).</ref>  That is, they assumed the velocity similarity scaling factor is given by:

:<math>
u_e(x)= U_0 \left( \frac x L \right)^m \quad ,
</math>  

where <math> L </math> is the wedge length and ''m'' is a dimensionless constant.  Falkner and Skan also assumed the boundary layer thickness scaling factor is proportional to:<ref>Schlichting, H., (1979). ''Boundary-Layer Theory'', 7th ed., McGraw-Hill, New York.</ref>{{rp|164}}   

:<math>
\delta (x) \; = \; \sqrt{\frac{2\nu L}{U_0(m+1)}}\left( \frac x L \right)^{(1-m)/2} \quad .
</math>
 
[[File:Falkskan.png|thumb|Falkner-Skan boundary layer profiles for selected values of <math>m</math>.]]

Mass conservation is automatically ensured when the Prandtl momentum boundary layer equations are solved using a [[stream function]] approach.  The stream function, in terms of the scaling factors, is given by:<ref>Panton, R., (2013). ''Incompressible Flow'', 4th ed., John Wiley, New Jersey.</ref>{{rp|543}} 

:<math>
\psi(x,y) \; = \; u_e(x)\delta(x)f(\eta) \quad ,
</math>

where <math>\eta = {y}/{\delta (x)} </math> and the velocities are given by:

:<math> 
u(x,y)\;  = \; \frac{{\partial \psi (x,y)}}{{\partial y}},\quad {\rm{and}}\quad v(x,y)\;  = \;  - \frac{{\partial \psi (x,y)}}{{\partial x}}\quad. 
</math>

This means

:<math>\psi(x,y) \; = \;  \sqrt{\frac{2\nu U_0 L}{m+1}}\left( \frac x L \right)^{(m+1)/2} f(\eta) \quad .</math>

The non-dimensionalized Prandtl ''x''-momentum equation using the similarity length and velocity scaling factors together with the stream function based velocities results in an equation known as the Falkner–Skan equation and is given by:

:<math>
f''' + f f'' + \beta \left[1-(f')^2 \right]=0  \quad ,
</math>

where each dash represents differentiation with respect to <math>\eta</math> (Note that another equivalent equation with a different <math>\beta</math> involving an <math>\alpha</math> is sometimes used. This changes ''f'' and its derivatives but ultimately results in the same backed-out <math>u(x,y)</math> and <math>v(x,y)</math> solutions).  This equation can be solved for certain <math>\beta</math> as an [[Ordinary differential equation|ODE]] with boundary conditions:
:<math>f(0)=f'(0)=0, \quad f'(\infty)=1.</math>

The wedge angle, after some manipulation, is given by:

: <math> \beta = \frac{2m}{m + 1} \quad. </math>

The <math>m = \beta = 0</math> case corresponds to the [[Blasius boundary layer]] solution. When <math>\beta=1</math>, the problem reduces to the [[Stagnation point flow#Hiemenz flow|Hiemenz flow]]. Here, ''m''&nbsp;<&nbsp;0 corresponds to an [[adverse pressure gradient]] (often resulting in [[boundary layer separation]]) while ''m''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0 represents a favorable pressure gradient. In 1937 [[Douglas Hartree]] showed that physical solutions to the Falkner–Skan equation exist only in the range <math>-0.090429\leq m \leq 2\ (-0.198838\leq\beta\leq 4/3)</math>. For more negative values of ''m'', that is, for stronger adverse pressure gradients, all solutions satisfying the boundary conditions at ''&eta;''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 have the property that ''f''(''&eta;'')&nbsp;>&nbsp;1 for a range of values of ''&eta;''. This is physically unacceptable because it implies that the velocity in the boundary layer is greater than in the main flow.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Stewartson|first1=K.|title=Further Solutions of the Falkner-Skan Equation|journal=Mathematical Transactions of the Cambridge Philosophical Society|date=3 December 1953|volume=50|issue=3|pages=454–465|doi=10.1017/S030500410002956X|s2cid=120914473 |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/C64E489495AC8D2B30B0DB7B5BF6E50E/S030500410002956Xa.pdf/div-class-title-further-solutions-of-the-falkner-skan-equation-div.pdf|accessdate=2 March 2017}}</ref> Further details may be found in Wilcox (2007).

With the solution for ''f'' and its derivatives in hand, the Falkner and Skan velocities become:<ref>Schlichting, H., (1979). ''Boundary-Layer Theory'', 7th ed., McGraw-Hill, New York.</ref>{{rp|164}}

:<math> u(x,y) = u_e(x)f' \quad ,</math>
and
:<math> v(x,y) = -\sqrt {\frac {(m+1) \nu U_0 }{2 L}  \left( \frac x L \right)^{m-1}} \left(f+\frac{m-1}{m+1}\eta f' \right)\quad .</math>

The Prandtl <math>y</math>-momentum equation can be rearranged to obtain the <math>y</math>-pressure gradient, <math>{\partial p}</math>/<math>{\partial y}</math>, (this is the formula<ref name="Aspects of Boundary Layer Theory">{{cite book|last=Weyburne |first=D. |date=February 2022 |title=Aspects of Boundary Layer Theory|url=https://sites.google.com/view/boundary-layer-theory/ |access-date=May 4, 2022 |isbn=978-0-578-98334-9|page=[https://sites.google.com/view/boundary-layer-theory/y-momentum-eq 46]}}</ref> appropriate for the <math>\alpha</math>=1 and <math>\beta</math>=2m/(m+1) case) as
:<math>
 \frac{{x^2 }}{{u_e^2 \delta _1 }}\frac{1}{\rho }\frac{{\partial p}}{{\partial y}}\;  = \;  - \frac{1 }{{4 }}(m+1)(3m - 1)f'' + \frac{1 }{{4 }}(m+1)(1 - m)\eta f''' - \frac{1}{4}(m + 1)^2 ff' + 
  \frac{1}{4}(m - 1)^2 \eta f'^2  -  \frac{1}{4}(m + 1)(m - 1)\eta ff'' \quad  \quad ,</math>


where the displacement thickness, <math>\delta_1</math>, for the Falkner-Skan profile is given by:

:<math>\delta_1 (x)= \left( \frac{2}{m+1}\right)^{1/2} \left( \frac{\nu x}{U}\right)^{1/2} \int_0^\infty (1-f') d\eta</math>

and the [[shear stress]] acting at the wedge is given by 

:<math>\tau_w (x)= \mu \left( \frac{m+1}{2}\right)^{1/2} \left( \frac{U^3}{\nu x}\right)^{1/2} f''(0) </math>

==Compressible Falkner–Skan boundary layer==

Source:<ref>Lagerstrom, Paco Axel. Laminar flow theory. Princeton University Press, 1996.</ref>

Here Falkner–Skan boundary layer with a specified [[specific enthalpy]] <math>h</math> at the wall is studied. The [[density]] <math>\rho</math>, [[viscosity]] <math>\mu</math> and thermal conductivity <math>\kappa</math> are no longer constant here. In the low [[Mach number]] approximation, the equation for conservation of mass, momentum and energy become

:<math>
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial (\rho u)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial (\rho v)}{\partial y} & = 0,\\
 \left(u \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + v \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} \right) & = - \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{dp}{dx} + \frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial }{\partial y} \left(\mu\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right),\\
\rho \left(u \frac{\partial h}{\partial x} + v \frac{\partial h}{\partial y} \right) &=  \frac{\partial }{\partial y} \left(\frac{\mu}{Pr} \frac{\partial h}{\partial y} \right) 
\end{align}
</math>

where <math>Pr=c_{p_\infty}\mu_\infty/\kappa_\infty</math> is the [[Prandtl number]] with suffix <math>\infty</math> representing properties evaluated at infinity. The boundary conditions become

:<math> u = v = h - h_w(x) = 0 \ \text{for} \ y=0</math>,
:<math> u -U = h - h_\infty =0 \ \text{for} \ y=\infty \ \text{or} \ x=0</math>.

Unlike the incompressible boundary layer, similarity solution can exists for only if the transformation

:<math>x\rightarrow c^2 x, \quad y\rightarrow cy, \quad u\rightarrow u, \quad v\rightarrow \frac{v}{c}, \quad h\rightarrow h, \quad \rho\rightarrow \rho, \quad \mu\rightarrow \mu</math>

holds and this is possible only if <math>h_w=\text{constant}</math>.

===Howarth transformation===

Introducing the self-similar variables using [[Howarth–Dorodnitsyn transformation]]

:<math>\eta = \sqrt{\frac{U_o(m+1)}{2\nu_\infty L^m}} x^{\frac{m-1}{2}}\int_0^y \frac{\rho}{\rho_\infty} dy, \quad \psi = \sqrt{\frac{2 U_o \nu_\infty}{(m+1) L^m}} x^{\frac{m+1}{2}} f(\eta), \quad \tilde h(\eta) = \frac{h}{h_\infty}, \quad \tilde h_w = \frac{h_w}{h_\infty}, \quad \tilde \rho = \frac{\rho}{\rho_\infty}, \quad \tilde \mu = \frac{\mu}{\mu_\infty}</math>

the equations reduce to 

:<math>
\begin{align}
(\tilde\rho\tilde \mu f'')' + ff'' + \beta [\tilde h - (f')^2] =0, \\
(\tilde\rho\tilde\mu \tilde h')' + Prf\tilde h'  =0 
\end{align}
</math>

The equation can be solved once <math>\tilde \rho = \tilde \rho(\tilde h),\ \tilde \mu = \tilde \mu(\tilde h)</math> are specified. The boundary conditions are

:<math>f(0)=f'(0)=\theta(0)-\tilde h_w=f'(\infty)-1=\tilde h(\infty)-1=0.</math>

The commonly used expressions for air are <math>\gamma = 1.4, \ Pr = 0.7, \ \tilde\rho = \tilde h^{-1}, \ \tilde\mu = \tilde h^{2/3}</math>. If <math>c_p</math> is constant, then <math>\tilde h=\tilde \theta = T/T_\infty</math>.
